newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-AGASSI HEADS INTO RETREAT WITH BOOS IN HIS EARS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-AGASSI HEADS INTO RETREAT WITH BOOS IN HIS EARS.

text.p: Andre Agassi headed into a six-week retreat from competitive tennis on Wednesday with the boos and whistles of angry, disappointed fans ringing in his ears.

For the second time within a month, Agassi faced a cacophony of jeers and whistles from German fans after a 6-3 6-4 defeat by Australian doubles expert Mark Woodforde in the first round of the Grand Slam Cup.

The chorus of disapproval was not as loud it was in Hanover last month when Agassi put up a spineless display against world number one Pete Sampras in the ATP world championship and promptly pulled out of the event, citing illness.

But Agassi admitted in Munich that he had been suffering with motivation problems in the last few months and needed a break from the game. The American has decided to miss next month's Australian Open.

"I certainly am taking the time off in the hope and desire and plan of getting strong, fit and getting my game back to where it can be," he said. "I seem to thrive in kind of digging myself in a bit of a hole and getting excited to come out of it again.
"None of it's worth it if you just keep running yourself into the ground, if you keep having to play events and keep chasing your tail."
Apart from winning an Olympic title and reaching the semifinals of the Australian and U.S. Opens, Agassi has done little to delight his numerous fans across the world this year.
The fans who paid up to 150 marks ($96) to watch his 76-minute performance were clearly not happy after Agassi made numerous unforced errors and served poorly.

They tried to lift his game with support throughout the match. But, by the end, they knew they were fighting a losing battle. Agassi said afterwards his main goal in the match was just making sure he hit the ball properly.

"Today I was just thinking about trying to make contact. It's a fast surface and I was worried about just making good, clear contact which would have been quite an accomplishment for me today," he said.

Agassi's game was littered with wild forehands and double faults and his timing was poor. Woodforde broke Agassi's serve as early as the second game after a double fault on his way to taking the first set in 34 minutes.

Although Agassi managed to find some good shots from the back of the court to get out of trouble at times, he effectively lost the match in the seventh game of the second set when he hit a backhand wide to drop his serve and give Woodforde a 4-3 lead.
The whistles and jeers started to get louder from then on. Agassi picked up $100,000 for the below-par performance at an event which pays out the biggest prize money in the sport.
In the first match of the day, big-serving Croat Goran Ivanisevic threw Swede Mikael Tillstrom out of the tournament with the subtlety of a night-club bouncer and grabbed a pay cheque of $262,500.
The defending champion put on a powerful display of aggressive serving to clinch a 6-4 6-2 victory in just 55 minutes.
Munich's indoor Olympic arena has witnessed some graceful sporting performances over the years, notably from gymnast Olga Korbut at the 1972 Games. But this was not one of them.
There were few rallies on the fast surface as both players hammered in serves of up to 200 kph. This was a performance of power, punch and little panache from the Croat.
